'''Alan Schriesheim''' is the Director [[Emeritus]] and the retired CEO<ref>{{cite web|url=http://argonne-national-laboratory.co.tv/ |accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222040717/http://argonne-national-laboratory.co.tv/ |archivedate=February 22, 2014 |title=Co.Tv }}</ref> of [[Argonne National Laboratory]], one of the [[U.S. Department of Energy]]'s largest research centers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anl.gov/Administration/index.html |title=About Argonne |accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514055504/http://www.anl.gov/Administration/index.html |archivedate=May 14, 2011 }}</ref> In a January 2008 announcement issued by [[Penn State University]] upon the establishment of the Schriesheim [[Distinguished Graduate Fellowship]], it was noted that "Schriesheim is an internationally acclaimed chemist and technology executive. With a career spanning 50 years in industry, academia, and government, Schriesheim was a pioneer in transforming large and highly complex research organizations to yield productive commercialized technology.<ref name="sc">{{cite web|url=http://www.science.psu.edu/alumni/recent-gift-announcements/schriesheim-gift-of-250-000-creates-distinguished|title=Schriesheim Gift of $250,000 Creates Distinguished Graduate Fellowship in Science|work=Psu.edu|accessdate=2015-04-08|archive-date=March 23, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323172445/http://science.psu.edu/alumni/recent-gift-announcements/schriesheim-gift-of-250-000-creates-distinguished|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="c2st">{{cite web|url=http://c2st.org/about/alan-schriesheim |title=Alan Schriesheim - Chicago Council on Science and Technology|accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110813004423/http://c2st.org/about/alan-schriesheim |archivedate=August 13, 2011 }}</ref>

== Early childhood and education ==
Alan Schriesheim was born in 1930 in [[Far Rockaway, Queens|Far Rockaway]], [[Queens]], New York. He graduated from [[Far Rockaway High School]] in 1948 where he played [[American football|football]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.farrockaway.com/football1945.html|title=Football Team 1945|work=Farrockaway.com|accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref> Schriesheim graduated from [[Penn State]] in 1954 with a PhD in [[chemistry]], having earned his bachelor's degree from The [[Polytechnic Institute of New York University]] (known then as Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute) in 1951. He was the first person in his family to attend college, his father had a 6th grade education and was a furniture store manager.<ref name="aip" />

==Career==
Schriesheim joined The National Bureau of Standards (renamed the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]]) as a research [[chemist]] immediately after graduating with his PhD and worked there from 1954 to 1956. Schriesheim joined [[Exxon]] in 1956 and worked there for 27 years until 1982, rising through the organization to become general manager of Exxon Engineering and director of Exxon Corporate Research.<ref name="aip">{{cite web|url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?schriesheima|title=Alan Schriesheim|work=Aip.org|accessdate=2015-04-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121006232754/http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?schriesheima|archive-date=October 6, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1983, he became director and CEO of the [[Argonne National Laboratory]], while also holding a dual appointment as a [[Professor of Chemistry]] at [[The University of Chicago]], retiring in 1996.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/951109/shriesheim.shtml|title=Argonne Director, CEO Schriesheim announces retirement|work=Uchicago.edu|accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref> He was the first director of a major national laboratory to have an extensive industrial background.<ref name="anl">{{cite web|url=http://www.anl.gov/Science_and_Technology/History/Anniversary_Frontiers/renewal.html |title=1984-1996: Years of Renewal|accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110122110138/http://www.anl.gov/Science_and_Technology/History/Anniversary_Frontiers/renewal.html |archivedate=January 22, 2011 }}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
[[File:SchriesheimReagan SuperconductivityLarge.gif|thumb|right|250px|[[Argonne National Laboratory|Argonne]] CEO Alan Schriesheim and U.S. President [[Ronald Reagan]] in 1987 during demonstration of high-temperature superconductivity (U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science)]]
While at Exxon, he won the [[American Chemical Society]]'s [[George Olah]] award for research in petroleum chemistry in 1969.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://portal.acs.org/portal/acs/corg/content?_nfpb=true&_pageLabel=PP_ARTICLEMAIN&node_id=1319&content_id=CTP_004526&use_sec=true&sec_url_var=region1&__uuid=54b3a151-31ff-4b3c-bafb-f6a0f24dc606|title=George A. Olah Award in Hydrocarbon or Petroleum Chemistry|work=Acs.org|accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref>

Schriesheim served on several public corporate boards, many university and government advisory committees, and is a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nae.edu/MembersSection/Directory20412/28602.aspx|title=NAE Website - Dr. Alan Schriesheim|work=Nae.edu|accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref> and holds 22 U.S. [[patents]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://alumni.psu.edu/awards/individual/daa/docs/2005-distinguished/Schriesheim.pdf |title=Alan Schriesheim '54g |publisher=Alumni.psu.edu |accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://cafefoundation.org/v2/pdf_tech/SATS.demographs/PAV.NRC.Report.NASA.Aero.pdf |title=Aeronautics Innovation : NASA's Challengers and Opportunities |publisher=Cafefoundation.org |accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref> He is a member of the board of directors of publicly traded [[HEICO]], an aerospace and defense electronics company, and was a former board member of Sun Electric Company<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1991/05/23/joins-sun-board-alan-schriesheim-director-of/|title=Joins Sun board: Alan Schriesheim, director of Argonne...|work=Chicago Tribune|date=May 23, 1991 |access-date=2015-04-08}}</ref> and of [[Rohm and Haas]] a [[Fortune 500]] chemical company.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.getfilings.com/o0000950154-96-000124.html|title=ROHM & HAAS CO - 10-K Annual Report - 12/31/1995|work=Getfilings.com|accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://people.forbes.com/profile/alan-schriesheim/40185|title=Alan Schriesheim|work=People.forbes.com|accessdate=2015-04-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120413211358/http://people.forbes.com/profile/alan-schriesheim/40185|archive-date=April 13, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He received several honorary doctorate degrees including a 2001 honorary degree in science from [[Penn State]], and in 2005 he was named a [[Distinguished Alumnus]], the highest honor the university can bestow on its graduates.<ref name="sc" /> He also holds honorary degrees from [[Penn State]], [[Illinois Institute of Technology]] and [[Northern Illinois University]]<ref name="c2st" /> and is a board member of [[Children's Memorial Hospital]] in Chicago, Illinois.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://in.reuters.com/finance/stocks/officerProfile?symbol=HEIa.N&officerId=103770 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121004193234/http://in.reuters.com/finance/stocks/officerProfile?symbol=HEIa.N&officerId=103770 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-10-04 |title=Officer Profile &#124; Quotes |publisher=In.reuters.com |date= |accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref> Dr. Schriesheim continues to reside in Chicago and is president of [https://www.c2st.org/about/ The Chicago Council on Science and Technology].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.medill.northwestern.edu/chicago/news.aspx?id=158591 |title=Alan Schriesheim: Chemist takes science to critical mass|accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140223102027/http://news.medill.northwestern.edu/chicago/news.aspx?id=158591 |archivedate=February 23, 2014 }}</ref>

In 1987, [[Argonne National Laboratory|Argonne]] Director and CEO Alan Schriesheim demonstrated [[high-temperature superconductivity]] to U.S. President [[Ronald Reagan]] at a 1987 superconductor applications meeting.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anl.gov/Science_and_Technology/History/Anniversary_Frontiers/64photo.html |title=President Reagan witnesses superconductivity|accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528121312/https://www.anl.gov/Science_and_Technology/History/Anniversary_Frontiers/64photo.html |archivedate=May 28, 2010 }}</ref> He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1989 for innovative chemical and chemical engineering research and for leadership in both the academic and the industrial sectors.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Alan Schriesheim |url=https://nae.edu/28602/Dr-Alan-Schriesheim |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=NAE Website |language=en}}</ref>

In 1996, Schriesheim became a Lincoln Laureate and was awarded The Order of Lincoln by [[The Lincoln Academy of Illinois]] – the highest honor awarded by the State of Illinois.<ref name="tlincoln">{{cite web|url=http://www.thelincolnacademyofillinois.org/laureates|title=The Honor Roll of Laureates|work=Thelincolnacademyofillinois.org|accessdate=2015-04-08}}</ref> Other notable Lincoln Laureates include 1981 Laureate U.S. President [[Ronald Reagan]], artist [[LeRoy Neiman]], [[Olympic Gold Medal]] winner [[Jacqueline Joyner-Kersee]], author [[Studs Terkel]], author [[Scott Turow]], scientist and [[Nobel Laureate]] [[Leon M. Lederman]], actor [[Charlton Heston]], writer and [[Nobel Laureate]] [[Saul Bellow]], architect [[Ludwig Mies van der Rohe]], .<ref name="tlincoln" />

According to the Official History of The Lincoln Academy:<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thelincolnacademyofillinois.org/order_of_lincoln |title=The Order of Lincoln |work=Thelincolnacademyofillinois.org |accessdate=2015-04-08 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150224223728/http://thelincolnacademyofillinois.org/order_of_lincoln |archivedate=February 24, 2015 |df=mdy }}</ref>

{{Blockquote|The Order of Lincoln was established in 1964 by Proclamation of Illinois Governor Otto Kerner to honor individuals whose contributions to the betterment of humanity have been accomplished in Illinois, or, whose achievements have brought honor to the state because of their identity with it, whether by birth or residence, or whose dedication to the principles of public service inspire all Illinoisans to respond to what Lincoln called 'the better angels of our nature'. To insure that no political connotation should surround the award, an independent, non-partisan entity was established to administer the program. Thus, the Order of Lincoln and the Lincoln Academy (based respectively upon the French Legion of Honor and the French Academy) were established, with Michael Butler, the Academy's first chancellor, as its primary architect. In 1989, as part of the Academy's twenty-fifth anniversary, Governor James R. Thompson declared the Order of Lincoln to be 'the state's highest award' and every Illinois Governor since then has so described it. Each honoree receives a warrant signed by the Governor and bearing the Great Seal of the State of Illinois, certifying his or her investiture as a Laureate of the Order of Lincoln.}}

== Family ==
He and Beatrice, his late wife of fifty years, met while they were both graduate students in Chemistry at [[Penn State]].<ref name="sc" /> Beatrice Schriesheim (née Brand)<ref>{{cite web|author= |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2003/09/04/schriesheim-beatrice-d-2/ |title=Schriesheim, Beatrice D. - tribunedigital-chicagotribune |publisher=Articles.chicagotribune.com |date=2003-09-04 |access-date=2015-04-08}}</ref> was born in 1930 in [[Poland]] and survived the [[Holocaust]] by escaping the [[Nazi]] invasion in 1939 and surviving imprisonment in [[Siberia]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2003-09-09 |title=BEATRICE SCHRIESHEIM, 73 |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2003/09/09/beatrice-schriesheim-73/ |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref> . She arrived in the U.S. in 1947 and received her undergraduate degree from [[Queens College, City University of New York|Queen's College]] in New York before attending [[Penn State]]'s Graduate School . She was a long-time high school chemistry teacher who was committed to her students as well as to the improvement of science education in the United States . She played a leadership role in the Achievement Rewards for College Scientists (ARCS) organization.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2003-09-09 |title=BEATRICE SCHRIESHEIM, 73 |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2003/09/09/beatrice-schriesheim-73/ |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref> Her memoirs, "Bea's Journey", documented her Holocaust journey and her life in the United States and are included in the [[United States Holocaust Memorial Museum]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schriesheim |first=Bea |date=2003 |title=Bea's Journey Memoirs |url=https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/bib94889 |website=United States Holocaust Museum}}</ref> . They were published in 2003 after her death at the age of 73.<ref>https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bea%27s_Journey_-_a_memoir_of_Beatrice_Schriesheim.pdf {{Dead link|date=February 2022}}</ref> She shared her husband's affection and enthusiasm for the university and for helping outstanding students through scholarship support. Alan and Bea Schriesheim had two children, Laura Lyn and [[Robert A. Schriesheim]], and six grandchildren.<ref name="sc" />

== Philanthropy ==
The Schriesheim Distinguished Graduate Fellowship,<ref name="sc" /> according to a press release issued by The [[Penn State University]], was established at [[Penn State University]] by [[Penn State]] alumnus Alan Schriesheim in January 2008 who gave $250,000 to the [[Eberly College of Science]] to create a Distinguished Graduate Fellowship.

According to the January 2008 [[Penn State]] press release, The fellowship, named for the donor and his late wife, Beatrice "Bea" Schriesheim, will help the [[Eberly College of Science]] to recruit academically talented first-year graduate students who are pursuing doctoral degrees, according to Dean Daniel Larson. First preference will be given to students majoring in chemistry.<ref name="sc" />

[[Penn State]]'s Distinguished Graduate Fellowship program<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gradsch.psu.edu/prospective/funding/programs/distingradfellowships.html |title=Distinguished Graduate Fellowships|accessdate=June 1, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090622175558/http://www.gradsch.psu.edu/prospective/funding/programs/distingradfellowships.html |archivedate=June 22, 2009 }}</ref> is a university-wide program that aims to attract the nation's most capable graduate students. When a fellowship is fully funded at its $250,000 minimum, the university, through the Graduate School and the fellowship's affiliate college, will match the endowment's annual spendable income in perpetuity, thus increasing the amount available to the recipient in the form of tuition aid, a stipend, and health insurance.<ref name="sc" />

“The Schriesheim Fellowship will have an impact that will last beyond our lifetimes and will influence bright students and future discoveries,” said Larson. “We are grateful to Alan for recognizing the value of such a fellowship to the Eberly College and to generations of its students.”<ref name="sc" />
